sub_hypo.relations: The SES logit coefficient changes from +0.4729 (p=1.04e-09) without controls to -0.2316 (p=0.0375; 95% CI [-0.450, -0.013]) with academic and race controls. sub_hypo.text: Academic ability and class percentile, rather than race alone, drive the reversal of the SES–BA completion association, a pattern interpreted as suppression of the academic-realized component of SES.
sub_hypo.context: The same complete NLS sample, comparing logistic models with academic controls, race controls, and both blocks; White is the initial race reference category.
sub_hypo.relations: Academic controls alone reverse the SES coefficient to -0.2171 (p=0.0436); race controls alone attenuate it to +0.3524 (p=7.5e-5); both blocks yield -0.2316. SES correlates positively with ASVAB (+0.463) and class percentile (+0.304), and negatively with Black (-0.152) and Hispanic (-0.251) indicators. Conditioning on academics is interpreted as removing the positively associated academic component of SES, leaving a negatively associated residual component; this is an interpretation, not an established causal mechanism.

sub_hypo.text: Adding family size and sex to the academic- and race-adjusted model reverses the SES coefficient back to positive in logistic regression, indicating sensitivity to accompanying family-background controls.
sub_hypo.context: The complete NLS sample; the fully adjusted logistic model uses White and Male reference categories, with an OLS/linear-probability cross-check.
sub_hypo.relations: Adding sex and family size changes the SES logit coefficient from -0.2316 to +0.2906 (p=0.0136), with an average marginal effect of +0.00690. Family size correlates negatively with ASVAB (-0.24) and class percentile (-0.15), but approximately zero with SES (+0.024); the hypothesis interprets its addition as reintroducing a suppressor channel. The fully adjusted OLS SES coefficient does not turn positive: it is -0.00129 and nonsignificant (p=0.66).

sub_hypo.text: BA completers have higher mean SES than non-completers within each racial group, with larger SES gaps among Black and Hispanic participants than among White participants.
sub_hypo.context: NLS participants grouped by White, Black, or Hispanic race and BA completion status; SES is compared with the overall mean of zero.
sub_hypo.relations: White completers and non-completers have mean SES +0.290 and +0.176, respectively, a gap of +0.114. Black participants have corresponding means +0.273 and -0.216, a gap of +0.489; Hispanic participants have means +0.002 and -0.458, a gap of +0.460. The hypothesis attributes a disproportionate share of the positive whole-sample association to minority participants having both lower SES and lower BA completion rates.

sub_hypo.text: The negative SES association after academic and race adjustment is robust to race-reference coding, conventional standard-error choices, and a probit link, but is only marginally statistically significant.
sub_hypo.context: The complete NLS sample under the model controlling for ASVAB, class percentile, and race; sensitivity checks change race references, standard-error estimation, and model link.
sub_hypo.relations: Changing the race reference among White, Black, and Hispanic leaves the SES logit coefficient at -0.2316 (HC1 p=0.0375). Nonrobust logistic standard errors give p=0.0211; probit gives a negative coefficient of -0.0939 (p=0.0395). OLS also reproduces the bivariate-to-adjusted sign change, from +0.01335 to -0.00632 (adjusted p=0.0389). These checks support a sign reversal, not the claimed loss of significance at the 5% threshold.
